1.6 — Animation States: IsWalking, WalkDir, Attack

Your character moves, but it does not look like it is moving — it slides around in the same idle pose whichever way you push. Today you fix that, and the fix is small: a script never plays an animation itself, it asks the Animator for one by setting parameters. You already have the input from 1.4 and 1.5. Everything you need to add is given below, one line at a time, with the reason for each one.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I play a walking animation?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

Play a walking animation — "how do I play a walking animation?" — for a character that already moves in four directions, with a different clip for each one and a picture that has to face the way it walks.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Get a handle on the Animator and the Sprite RendererTwo fields in the class body, filled once in Start(). Both components live on the child Sprite rather than on the Player, so plain GetComponent finds nothing: this part is GetComponentInChildren, and getting it wrong is a NullReferenceException the moment you press a direction key.Read: the Animator and sprite.flipX rows in the quick reference, and the child Sprite you met in 1.2.
  2. Work out whether the player is moving at allOne true/false value built out of the two input fields 1.4 gave you: inputX != 0f || inputY != 0f. Hand it to the Animator as IsWalking, and the controller decides whether that means idle or walking. You never name a clip.Read: the anim.SetBool("IsWalking", b) row in the quick reference, and the Parameters tab of the Animator window.
  3. Work out which direction the player is facingCompare the two inputs by size rather than by sign, which is what Mathf.Abs does for you — walking hard left is -1 and would lose to a gentle nudge upward otherwise. The winner picks the clip through WalkDir: 0 up, 1 sideways, 2 down.Read: the Mathf.Min / Max / Abs / FloorToInt row in the quick reference, and the transition arrows you read in the Animator window.
  4. Turn the picture around to match the directionThe controller has one sideways walk clip and it is drawn facing right, so the sprite is mirrored rather than a second clip drawn: an if statement sets spriteRenderer.flipX to true when the player is pushing left, and back to false when they are pushing right. Only the sideways branch needs it, because the up and down clips face the camera.Read: the sprite.flipX = b row in the quick reference.

Notice the shape: one part finds the machine, one asks a yes/no question, one asks a which-one question, and one turns the picture around. Animation looks like a whole new subject and it is four decisions — and only the first of them needs a look-up, because the other three are the input fields from 1.4 being asked questions about themselves.

The test: does the part name an API you could search for? "Play the walking animation" cannot be looked up. SetBool, SetInteger and flipX can — and each of them is a part.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

The walkthrough also fires an attack with SetTrigger, and a swing is not one of the parts above. Why is it not part of "play a walking animation", and what is different about an action that ends by itself?

Two methods are written in the walkthrough and neither one runs until something calls it. Where in Update() do those calls belong, and why would calling them before the input is read animate the wrong frame?

In 1.4 you read inputX and inputY once per frame and used them to move the character. Today those same two numbers answer two questions — is anything moving, and which way is it facing. What is different about what the numbers are being used for?

In 1.3 you learned that a reference kept in the class body survives, while one declared inside a method does not. Which part above is that rule doing the work in, and what does the Console say when you break it?

In 1.5 you made the direction vector's length exactly 1 so that pushing two keys could not make you faster. Today you compare how hard each axis is being pushed. What does Mathf.Abs throw away so the comparison is about strength rather than direction — and why does walking left lose to a gentle nudge upward without it?

Read the Docs ~12 min

In professional game engines, scripts rarely swap individual sprite images. The visual side is handled by an Animator Controller — a visual state machine with clips for idle, for walking in each direction, and for the attack. Your C# script communicates with it by setting parameters, and the controller decides which clip that means. These are the methods that do the talking:

Unity APISignatureBehaviour
animator.SetBool() void SetBool(string name, bool value) Sets a boolean parameter. For persistent, continuous states — idle versus walking. True and false are both meaningful values.
animator.SetInteger() void SetInteger(string name, int value) Sets a whole-number parameter. For discrete multi-state selection such as a direction (0, 1, 2). Each value is a different clip.
animator.SetFloat() void SetFloat(string name, float value) Sets a decimal parameter, for smooth values such as speed, or a point on a walk-to-run blend. The fourth member of this family — this controller has no Float parameter, so you will not call it today, but you will meet it later.
animator.SetTrigger() void SetTrigger(string name) Fires a momentary trigger, which resets itself once a transition consumes it. For one-shot actions such as attacks or jumps. No value is passed — being fired is the whole message.
spriteRenderer.flipX bool (read/write) Mirrors the sprite horizontally. Lets one sideways walk animation serve both left and right.
Mathf.Abs() float Mathf.Abs(float f) Returns a number's absolute value, stripping the sign. For comparing magnitudes regardless of direction.
GetComponentInChildren<T>() T GetComponentInChildren<T>() Finds a component on this GameObject or on any of its children. You need this one today — remember where the Sprite Renderer and the Animator turned out to live.

One thing this table cannot tell you: the names in those quoted strings. A parameter name is not a Unity keyword — it is a name somebody typed into this project's controller, and your string has to match it exactly.

Socratic: Separation of Concerns

  1. Why does your script set abstract parameters like "IsWalking" rather than telling the engine "play frame 4 of the walk sprite sheet"?
  2. If an artist replaced a 4-frame walk animation with an 8-frame one, how much C# would have to change? What does your answer say about the value of this split?
  3. What is the technical difference between setting a boolean with SetBool and firing an action with SetTrigger? Which one resets itself, and why does that matter for an attack?
  4. The Animator and the Sprite Renderer are both on the child object, while your script is on the parent. Why would GetComponent<Animator>() return nothing, and what does GetComponentInChildren<Animator>() do differently?
Inspect the Controller You Are Driving ~10 min

Before you write a line, go and read the machine you are about to talk to. Someone built this state machine for you; your job is only to drive it, and you cannot drive something you have not looked at. In the Overworld scene, select the child Sprite object under Player — from 1.2, that is where the Animator lives, not on the Player root — then open Window → Animation → Animator.

  1. Click the Parameters tab in the top-left of the Animator window. Three parameters are already configured: IsWalking (Bool), WalkDir (Int), and Attack (Trigger). What are the exact spellings, including capitals? Write them down — you will type them into strings, and Unity will not forgive a typo.
  2. Click the arrow from Walk_Horiz to Idle_Horiz and read its condition in the Inspector. Which parameter does it test, and what value does it want?
  3. Click the arrows between the up, side, and down states. They compare WalkDir to 0, 1, and 2. Which number means which direction? You need these exact values in your code, and the wrong one is a character that walks backwards.
  4. Now click the arrow into any of the Shovel_Swing states. What two conditions must both be true before the attack animation plays?
  5. Look at the Animator component in the Inspector. Which controller asset is assigned to it, and what kind of parameter — Bool, Int, Float, or Trigger — is missing from this controller entirely?
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I play a walking animation?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. You already have movement from 1.4 and 1.5 — a character that moves but never changes pose. You will now add the animation half of the script, and every line of it is given and explained below.

Step 1Declare the two components at class scope

Your script can only talk to a component it holds a reference to. Two components decide what you see: the Animator, which plays clips, and the Sprite Renderer, which is the picture itself. Add a field for each, directly under the fields you already have.

    private Animator animator;
    private SpriteRenderer spriteRenderer;
  1. 1A field that will hold the Animator component. Notice it has no value yet — Start() gives it one in the next step.It goes in the class body, not inside a method, for exactly the reason from 1.3: a reference kept here is found once and remembered for the whole game. A reference declared inside Update() would be thrown away and looked up again sixty times a second.
  2. 2The same thing for the picture. You need it for one single line later in this walkthrough — flipX — but it still has to be a field, so Start() can fill it in once.Both fields start as null, which means "nothing at all". Every NullReferenceException in this lesson comes from a field that was declared but never assigned.

Step 2Find them once, in Start()

Start() runs once, before the first frame. That is the right place to look a component up — Update() would repeat the search every single frame.


    void Start()
    {
        animator = GetComponentInChildren<Animator>();
        spriteRenderer = GetComponentInChildren<SpriteRenderer>();
    }
  1. 2The lifecycle method from 1.3. Unity calls it for you, exactly once, before the first frame runs.
  2. 3Opens Start().
  3. 4Searches the Player and every object beneath it for an Animator, and stores the first one it finds in the field you just declared.This is the line that catches everyone. The Animator is not on the Player — it is on the child Sprite, the split you met back in 1.2. Plain GetComponent<Animator>() looks only at the object this script sits on, so it finds nothing and returns null.
  4. 5Exactly the same shape, and for the same reason: the picture also lives on the child Sprite, not on the Player root.
  5. 6Closes Start(). Both fields now hold a real component, and they will keep holding it for the rest of the game.

Step 3Write UpdateAnimation() and set the walking flag

Now your own method, called once per frame. It answers one question first: is the player moving at all? All four directions share that answer, so it is settled before anything else.


    void UpdateAnimation()
    {
        bool isMoving = inputX != 0f || inputY != 0f;
        animator.SetBool("IsWalking", isMoving);
  1. 2A method you write yourself. void means it hands nothing back when it finishes. Nothing calls it automatically — you will add the call from Update() in step 7.Animation in its own method is what keeps Update() readable as three ideas: read the input, move the character, update the visuals. That is the separation of concerns the Read the Docs section asked you to argue for.
  2. 3Opens UpdateAnimation(). Every line until its closing brace runs sixty times a second.
  3. 4Builds a bool — a true/false value — out of the two input fields 1.4 gave you. != means "is not equal to", and || means "or". Read the whole line as: horizontal input is not zero or vertical input is not zero.This is the first time those two fields have been used for anything except movement. Standing still is 0 on both axes, so isMoving is false exactly when no direction key is held.
  4. 5The new API. It hands the Animator a named parameter and a true/false value, and the Animator Controller decides which clip that means. You never name a clip or a frame in code — that is the whole point of the split.The name in quotes has to match a parameter in the controller character for character. "IsWalking" here, with a capital I and a capital W, because that is how it is spelled in the Animator window.

Step 4Choose the direction with Mathf.Abs

The controller has three directional states and one integer parameter, WalkDir, to choose between them: 0 for up, 1 for sideways, 2 for down. Diagonal movement is the interesting case — you are pushing two axes at once, and only one clip can play.


        if (Mathf.Abs(inputX) >= Mathf.Abs(inputY))
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 1);
        }
        else if (inputY > 0f)
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 0);
        }
        else
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 2);
        }
  1. 2Compares the sizes of the two inputs. Mathf.Abs throws the sign away, so -1 is counted as 1. >= means "greater than or equal to". If horizontal wins this test, the sideways clip is the one that plays.Without Mathf.Abs, walking hard left (-1) would lose to a gentle nudge upward (+0.2) and your character would face the wrong way. You are comparing how hard the player is pushing, not which way is positive.
  2. 3Opens the sideways branch — everything here runs when horizontal movement dominates.
  3. 4SetInteger is the setter for an Int parameter. In this controller 1 means "walking sideways", so this is the line that selects the side-on clip.
  4. 5Closes the sideways branch.
  5. 6Only reached when horizontal did not win. > 0f asks whether the vertical axis is positive: up is +1, down is -1.else if is checked only when the first condition failed, so the two branches can never both run. This is a decision tree, and each question gets asked once, in order.
  6. 7Opens the upward branch.
  7. 80 means walking up in this controller.
  8. 9Closes the upward branch.
  9. 10Everything left over. If it was not sideways and it was not up, the only direction remaining is down.
  10. 11Opens the downward branch.
  11. 122 means walking down. Those three numbers — 0, 1, 2 — are not yours to invent; they are the values the transition arrows compare against.
  12. 13Closes the downward branch, and the if / else if / else chain with it.Standing still: both inputs are 0, so this chain runs anyway and WalkDir ends up as 1. That is harmless — the Idle state does not look at WalkDir at all. It only matters while IsWalking is true.

Step 5Mirror the sprite for left and right

The controller has one sideways walk clip, drawn facing right. Rather than a second clip for the other direction, Unity mirrors the picture. That is the Sprite Renderer's job, not the Animator's — and it is the reason you cached a second component in step 2.


        if (Mathf.Abs(inputX) >= Mathf.Abs(inputY))
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 1);

            if (inputX < 0f)
            {
                spriteRenderer.flipX = true;
            }
            else
            {
                spriteRenderer.flipX = false;
            }
        }
  1. 2Already in your file from the last step — the same sideways test. It is repeated here only so you can see where the new line goes.
  2. 3Opens the sideways branch again.
  3. 4Already written. 1 selects the side-on walk clip.
  4. 6The new line. It asks one yes/no question: is the player pushing left? inputX goes negative when they hold the left key, so inputX < 0f — "less than zero" — is true to the left and false to the right.Only the sideways branch needs this. The up and down clips are drawn facing the camera, so there is no left or right version of them to choose between. Flipping while walking up would change nothing you can see, and it would be one more line of code to explain.
  5. 7Opens the "pushing left" block. Exactly the same shape as the sideways branch you are already standing inside.
  6. 8flipX is a true/false property on the Sprite Renderer: true mirrors the picture left-to-right, so the character faces left. Writing the value out by name — = true — rather than squeezing the whole thing into one expression means there is nothing to decode when you read the line back.
  7. 9Closes the "pushing left" block.
  8. 10Everything the question did not catch: the player is pushing right.
  9. 11Opens the "pushing right" block.
  10. 12false leaves the picture unmirrored — which is how the sideways clip was drawn, facing right. This is the line that turns the sprite back the moment they push the other way.
  11. 13Closes the "pushing right" block, and the if / else nested inside the sideways branch with it.
  12. 14Closes the sideways branch. The up and down branches below it are untouched.

Step 6Fire the attack with a trigger

An attack is not a state the player stays in — it is a one-shot. The controller has a Trigger parameter for exactly this, and a trigger clears itself once a transition has consumed it. Clicking the mouse is a question about input, not about animation, so it gets its own method.


    void CheckAttack()
    {
        if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))
        {
            animator.SetTrigger("Attack");
        }
    }
  1. 2A second method of your own, for the same reason as UpdateAnimation(): attacking is not walking, and tangling the two makes both harder to read. Like UpdateAnimation(), nothing calls it until you say so.
  2. 3Opens CheckAttack().
  3. 4Input again, the class from 1.4 — but asking about the mouse this time. Button 0 is the left mouse button. GetMouseButtonDown is true on the single frame the button goes down.Input.GetMouseButton(0), without the Down, is true on every frame the button is held. Use that one here and the swing restarts sixty times a second, which looks like a broken animation rather than a broken condition.
  4. 5Opens the "the mouse was clicked this frame" block.
  5. 6Fires the trigger. Notice it takes only a name — no value, because a trigger has no state to set. The Animator plays the swing and resets the trigger when it is finished.
  6. 7Closes the click block.
  7. 8Closes CheckAttack().

Step 7Call both helpers from Update()

Both methods are written and neither one runs yet. A method you write yourself does nothing until something calls it, and Update() is the only thing in your script that runs every frame.

        transform.Translate(movement);

        UpdateAnimation();
        CheckAttack();
  1. 1Your existing movement line from 1.4 and 1.5 — leave it exactly where it is.
  2. 3Runs the animation logic every frame. The parentheses are empty because the method needs nothing handed to it: inputX and inputY are fields, so they are already sitting there for it to read.The position matters. Put this call after the input is read, not before. isMoving and WalkDir are built from inputX and inputY, so calling it earlier would animate last frame's input and the character would visibly lag behind its own movement.
  3. 4The same idea for the attack. It has to be here inside Update() — Start() runs once, and the player can click at any moment.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • declaring private Animator animator; and never giving it a value — no Start(), or a Start() that only handles other things

    You will seeThe game runs, the character still moves, and then the moment you press a direction key the Console fills with NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object.

    Do thisA declared field is null until something assigns it. Add void Start() and put animator = GetComponentInChildren<Animator>(); inside it. Start() runs once before the first frame, so the lookup happens once rather than sixty times a second.

  • animator = GetComponent<Animator>(); — the version without InChildren

    You will seeThe same NullReferenceException, even though you can see the Animator component sitting right there in the Inspector when you select the Sprite object.

    Do thisThe Animator is on the child Sprite, not on the Player where this script lives. GetComponent<T>() looks only at the object the script is attached to, so it returns null. GetComponentInChildren<T>() searches that object and everything beneath it, which is why this lesson uses it for both the Animator and the Sprite Renderer.

  • animator.SetBool("isWalking", isMoving); — lowercase i — or "Walking", or "Walk"

    You will seeNothing happens visually. The character keeps sliding around in its idle pose, and somewhere in the Console there is a warning like Animator does not have a parameter named "isWalking". It does not crash, so it is very easy to miss.

    Do thisOpen the Animator window, click the Parameters tab, and copy the name exactly: IsWalking, capital I, capital W. Unity compares the string character for character; near enough is not enough.

  • animator.SetFloat("WalkDir", inputX); or animator.SetBool("WalkDir", true); — using a setter that does not match the parameter declared in the controller

    You will seeThe same quiet warning and no change on screen. WalkDir is an Int, so only SetInteger can move it.

    Do thisRead the parameter type in the Parameters tab and pick the matching method: SetBool for Bool, SetInteger for Int, SetFloat for Float, SetTrigger for Trigger. The word after Set is the type. This controller has no Float parameter at all, which is why you never call SetFloat here.

  • writing UpdateAnimation() but never calling it from Update()

    You will seeThe character moves and collides exactly as before, but the sprite is frozen in whatever pose it started in. No errors, nothing in the Console.

    Do thisA method you write yourself does nothing until something calls it. Update() is the only thing running every frame, so both calls belong at the end of it, after the input has been read.

  • if (Input.GetMouseButton(0)) instead of if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))

    You will seeHolding the mouse button makes the swing restart every frame — the shovel never finishes its arc. It reads as a broken animation rather than a broken condition.

    Do thisGetMouseButtonDown is true on the one frame the button goes down. GetMouseButton is true on every frame it is held. A one-shot trigger wants the single frame.

Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare this against your own file rather than pasting it in. Three things are worth checking closely: that both components are assigned in Start() with GetComponentInChildren, that UpdateAnimation() and CheckAttack() are both actually called from Update(), and that the three parameter names — IsWalking, WalkDir, Attack — match the Animator window character for character.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;

    private float inputX;
    private float inputY;

    private Animator animator;
    private SpriteRenderer spriteRenderer;

    void Start()
    {
        animator = GetComponentInChildren<Animator>();
        spriteRenderer = GetComponentInChildren<SpriteRenderer>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(inputX, inputY);
        direction = direction.normalized;

        Vector2 movement = direction * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;

        transform.Translate(movement);

        UpdateAnimation();
        CheckAttack();
    }

    void UpdateAnimation()
    {
        bool isMoving = inputX != 0f || inputY != 0f;
        animator.SetBool("IsWalking", isMoving);

        if (Mathf.Abs(inputX) >= Mathf.Abs(inputY))
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 1);

            if (inputX < 0f)
            {
                spriteRenderer.flipX = true;
            }
            else
            {
                spriteRenderer.flipX = false;
            }
        }
        else if (inputY > 0f)
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 0);
        }
        else
        {
            animator.SetInteger("WalkDir", 2);
        }
    }

    void CheckAttack()
    {
        if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))
        {
            animator.SetTrigger("Attack");
        }
    }
}
Test It, Then Break It ~25 min

Save your script, return to Unity, press Play, and walk in all four directions. Your character should blend between idle, walking sideways, walking up, and walking down, with the sprite flipping as it changes direction. Click the mouse to swing. Once that works, the section below is where you prove you know why — by breaking one piece at a time and predicting what will happen before you press Play.

Bug Hunt: Diagnosing Animation Faults

  1. Misspell "IsWalking" as "isWalking" (lowercase i). What does the Unity Console report? Why is a misspelled parameter a warning rather than a crash — and why is that a mixed blessing for a beginner?
  2. Delete the UpdateAnimation(); call from Update() and press Play. No errors appear and the character still moves. What does it look like, and what does that prove about methods you write yourself?
  3. Comment out both spriteRenderer.flipX lines — true and false. Walk left. Which way is the sprite facing now, and can any input make it face the other way while walking sideways?
  4. Change GetComponentInChildren<Animator>() to GetComponent<Animator>(). What error appears — and which line does Unity point at, the one in Start() or the one in UpdateAnimation()? What does the answer tell you about when the null was created and when it was first used?
  5. Set WalkDir to 7 — a value no transition in the controller checks. What happens to the animation, and what does that teach you about a state machine with no matching transition?
  6. Click the mouse rapidly, then hold it down instead. Describe the difference between the two, and connect it to GetMouseButtonDown versus GetMouseButton.

Tinker: Exploring state transitions

  1. Keep the Animator window open while the game runs in Play mode. Walk around. Watch the blue progress bar slide across each state and the transition arrows light up in real time. Which state is active when you stand still, and which parameter is it testing?
  2. Hold W and D together and watch WalkDir in the Parameters tab. Which branch of your if chain won, and what would you change in the condition if you wanted vertical movement to win instead?
  3. Your Player is wired to Player_Shovel.controller, which is why the attack is a shovel swing. Go and find Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/PlayerAnimator/Axe/Player_Axe.controller and open it. It is a complete, working controller with axe swings instead of shovel swings, and it is assigned to nothing. Which single property on the Animator component would you change to make your character swing an axe? (You will do exactly this in Unit 5.)
  4. Add a fourth parameter of your own to the controller and wire a transition to it. What is the minimum you need — a parameter, a state, and what else?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Open the Animator window and inspect states, arrows, and parameter conditions
  • Explain the distinct purposes of SetBool, SetInteger, SetFloat, and SetTrigger — and why the setter must match the parameter's type
  • Explain the architecture split: your code sets state parameters, the Animator Controller plays the clips
  • Say which WalkDir integer means up, sideways, and down
  • Use Mathf.Abs() to resolve which directional input dominates
  • Explain why GetComponent<Animator>() returns null on the Player, and why GetComponentInChildren does not
  • Cache component references in Start() rather than looking them up every frame
  • Commit your working animation integration to GitHub
